Sunrider Liberation Day has a very different feel compared to Mask of Arcadius (previous game). That said, if you were engaged by the previous game, you will most likely still like this.

Liberation Day's story is a bit more negative than the previous story, and puts less emphasis on the space opera daring captain and his ragtag crew, and focuses more on intrigue and betrayal. I personally think this was all executed very well, and this game fully engaged me (I have been swallowed whole by the Sunrider franchise).

Liberation Day has a different feel from MoA because you have your degree of control removed, while you watch the events of the main story arc play out. Apparently, this was controversial, which I have been told is why the developers released the Captain's Edition, which reworked the ending, as well as added REturn, which is a time-travelling arc separate from the main storyline.

I can definitely say that I really like the intrigue of the main storyline, and I also have enjoyed the routes in REturn I have played insofar. I like how the clear actions and consequences contrasts with the main game, and I must admit I am a fan of the whole time-travelling theme.

On the technical side, I really like the new artstyle. It adds new depth, and in my opinion is superior to Mask of Arcadius. The voiceacting took me a little while to get used to (especially after listening to their voices in English in the first game), but it's grown on me, and I am definitely a fan now.

Some minor changes were made to gameplay, such as animation removal, and some other minor changes, but the core features are essentially identical to MoA, including difficulty customisability. The gameplay still possesses the clunkiness of the previous game, but I still enjoyed it.

Would recommend.

I had sought to start playing this game many times but, having forgotten all about Sunrider except the fact I liked it as a teen, I decided to replay the first entry; while the art was a bit crude and the gameplay very meh, the world and its narrative left me wanting to see more of Kayto and crew, so here I am, beginning my final steps of this decade long journey with a sci-fi series I was not expecting to grow so fond of.
First of, Liberation Day steps up both in its audio and graphics: the sounds are clearer, the backgrounds look better and the models don't look so stiff. The girls have more detail to them especially in their hair but they still resemble their original versions, which is nice. The only model that did not change was Admiral Grey's and that was quite jarring.
The UI got a bit of an overhaul but the battle system stayed roughly the same with just small changes and add ons (the captain points have a limit, repairs cost way more, etc); they did take out the close ups for the battles though which makes the fights less cinematic; not really a problem since the cutscenes themselves got a big level up: particle effects, nicer looking art and voice acting of an all new japanese cast. The casting is ok with most voices fitting the characters but hearing Asaga go from "IMMA FIRE MA LAZER" to cute generic anime girl was a bit sad.
The music is still good with an opening that goes very hard but I could not believe when they used the spinning monkeys theme AGAIN in more than one scene.
Unfortunately the game is not accomodating for new people, expecting you to know what happened on the last game and to have played it to completion: this would not be a big thing if not for the fact that the game throws you into combat against a lot of enemies with the same difficulty the last game's final missions had.

Now, for the story: unfortunately for Sunrider, the sequel steers away from the original Mobile Suit Gundam and isntead feels heavily inspired by Mobile Suit Gundam SEED. Gone are the politics of the Alliance with the only interesting politic being the divide between the two factions of PACT; the main theme is now the harem, of which you have no way of choosing who to go to. They push the Kayto-Chigara relationship even though the most popular girl by the end of the original game was Ava all for plot reasons.
Speaking of plot, while it is definitely better paced than the last game and has some interesting ideas (first and foremost the idea of the Sharr being some sort of weird possession that happens to Ryuvia royalty, shame it never gets brought up again, but also the companionship between Sola and Asaga) the fact that ALL of it, the entire fate of this franchise galaxy, depended on a love triangle was not the kind of thing I was expecting and I don't mean that in a good way.
The way they use Chigara and Lynn in the story, how Asaga feels by the end and the whole thing about time paradoxes feels... off. This could have been a less complicated story and have benefited for it.
That last stand of the Sunrider though? That was exquisite to watch.

I'll keep my eyes open for the series going forward (there is a Sunrider 4 which I might just buy) but I am more cautious for Sunrider than I was when I finished Mask of Arcadius; the way the plot is moving might just make everything I liked about this series fall apart.

First off, if for some reason you've stumbled upon this game and haven't played Mask of Arcadius, go do so before considering this game.  You have options at the beginning of the game to select how your previous game went down if you didn't complete the game, but without backstory or context it will make no sense.  Besides, you would be playing this game but for free, and then you could give your money to this developer by purchasing this game.

As such, as a $25 game, it's not bad...but it's not especially grand either.  The combat system is only slightly more polished than the previous game, but I actually had the game crash on me once and two battles I had to tell it to reload (it threw an error but if you look at the bottom there's a reload button and after I hit it the game worked fine).  So it feels a little sad paying for a sequel that feels a bit janky, at least with the first game it was free so I can overlook some issues.  The way command points are earned and work in combat is probably the biggest difference, it actually encourages command point usage and more aggressive combat so that's a nice plus.  Nothing broke my computer and maybe I'm just a bit impatient during the battles, so if you played Mask of Arcadius and expected something different this time, other than command points, it will disappoint you.

The story of the first game (I'll try to keep it spoiler free), maybe not Shakespeare or the best story, but I was very interested in how things would play out.  You had plenty of choices, oftentimes it didn't seem matter, but some choices actually will help or harm you in this game.  But the choices seem very limited to the "main story" of this game, you don't feel very in control, you feel like you're watching a train wreck in slow motion.  In some ways it makes it fascinating, but in others you don't feel like the choices you've made matter anymore.  You're watching the character you tried to form with your choices go in a direction that you aren't sure you can agree with especially when your choices in the previous game don't seem to match.  Howbeit, once you complete the main story line that's when things get weird.  I can't fully explain it without spoilers, but let's just say you get a chance to change things.  So, if you've enjoyed the previous game's story, this one takes things in an...interesting direction.

Despite all these criticisms, I got the game on sale for $7.50 or so and I still enjoyed it, especially now that its sequel is out you can experience the full story.  So if this game goes on sale or is part of a nice bundle, definitely buy it, but I wouldn't drop $25 on it especially when the sequel is going to cost $30.  But if you'll drop $70+ on a brand new game without blinking and you enjoyed Mark of Arcadius then you could do far worse.

Just finished my playthrough (Captain difficulty). Tough to review. 
Long story short, strongly recommended based on the sci-fi tactical combat side, strongly recommended [b]against [/b] based on the story, which is an utter dog's breakfast and one of the worst video game stories I've ever experienced. I call it 4/5 for the combat (would be 5/5 if it weren't horribly laggy), 0/5 for the "visual novel".

First the good: 
the combat is polished from Mask of Arcadius, with some of the obvious cheesy tricks like Short Range Warp + Vanguard spam nerfed into oblivion, damage types rebalanced, and Asaga getting some needed TLC to address her shortcomings in MoA. The between mission prep was also improved: letting mech upgrades be sold back for 100% value permits more flexibility and experimentation; splitting Sunrider/ryder upgrade currency and mercenary/consumable currency gave you a better reason to use both to the fullest (I beat MoA without ever buying a torpedo).  That half of the game was excellent and I fully enjoyed the missions.  The music and art was quite good as well.

The bad: 
The combat screen is horribly unoptimised, with unit selection painfully laggy, voice lines and sound effects causing the music to stutter. This definitely hampered my enjoyment of the combat.  They took out the weapon fire splash screens from MoA because people complained they wasted time, but the lag wastes far more in this game. That said, the story is [u]much[/u] worse. 
 It is egregious because I was promised challenging tactical mecha combat combined with a waifu visual novel, but a visual novel implies the ability to make choices, even follow different routes!  ...and this had no choices and one route, with a railroaded romance which forced you, the protagonist, to act like a moron, insult your oldest friend, and generally break the character established in Mask of Arcadius (and virtually everyone else is jarringly out of character compared to the first game as well).  Every single chapter, practically every single scene, made the story worse and demonstrated the complete lack of editing even further. The ending was such a catastrophe that I was left sputtering in disbelief, my brain trying to comprehend what it had been forced to endure.  Right now, even if the next Sunrider game comes out, I have a hard time envisioning playing it, because that would mean remembering this story, and I'm already forcing it out of my brain with synthwave and cheap whiskey.

Sunrider LB is a the 2nd game in the series. It is a heavily anime-inspired narrative game combined with some space mech combat (it's just units on space hexes shooting at various things) and resource management, with an emphasis on a branching plot / mixed with a sorta dating sim (!?). It can be also described as "romance visual novel / stat management game".  If you have seen "overly dramatic emotions" a la Gundam (various incarnations) or Macross (or its derivative Robotech in the US) and similar genres, you'll understand the style. It can be off-putting to some as there are a few scenes of gratuitous nudity or slightly lewd situations. But those who wish for a way to participate in such drama will get their chance here. 

Sunrider LD is actually the 2nd game in the series, preceded by "Sunrider: Mask of Arcadius" (which is free!), and the prequel, Sunrider Academy.  In LD, Captain Kayto Shields, in command of prototype mecha carrier Sunrider, must lead his crew of "Ryder" (mech) pilots to liberate his home system of Cera from the "evil" PACT, only to discover even deeper mysteries...

The battle is fought on a hex grid, where the units, take turns to shoot at each other, one side, then the other. When it's your turn, each unit has a number of action points. Choose an action (with action point cost) until you either run out of ammo or action points, then go on to the next unit. Some shots, like missile barrage, can be partially intercepted by any friendly units in its way. Others, like laser, cannot. Some units have unique abilities such as buff or debuff, taunt (gets all enemies to target it). Some weapons are ryder busters while some weapons are ship killer. It is up to you to deploy the right ones at the right time. 

Between missions, you get to apply mission bounty (for kills, mainly) to improve your ryders and your ship. Extra weapons, more HP, more armor, you get the idea. You also get animated scenes among your crew mates, between you and the crewmate, as well as expository scenes regarding your enemy, gritting their teeth upon another of their plots foiled by you, but they have yet another plan... 

You are often asked to choose sides, and this will affect your relationship with the seven Ryder pilots, which, adding to the combat results, will obviously affect the plot progression. 

As mentioned before, there are occasional scenes of nudity or teasing lewdness. So this is NOT for kids. 

If you have played the previous game (which is free on Steam, BTW) you can import your choices... Or you can just "choose" your decisions and see how those choices affect your current playthrough. 

In fact, the developer also added a [Re]launch option after you complete a playthrough, which adds a time-travel narrative that let's you explore OTHER decision points and their consequences... 

The graphics are decent, but the combat is slightly graphically underwhelming. The tactical combat however, is pretty good, as different ryders (mecha) do feel different. One's a "tank" with lots of armor, one's a ninja low on health but huge damage on mobility and melee, one's a sniper with a long-range grav rifle, one's a support with the ability to buff and debuff... It's up to you to deploy them optimally to defeat your enemies. 

All in all, if you like the idea of participating in a "visual novel" of mecha combat, definitely give the free version a try, then decide if you want this version.
